clue.text: Mate joining ace band pleased as Punch

parts.note: 'cock' is an old British form of address between men, like 'mate'
A is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards
a hoop is a circular band

explanation.surface: A friend who has just got into a top band is thrilled about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ace band' reads as a single phrase for a great group, but it splits into the card abbreviation and a ring-shaped band.
explanation.definitionFit: Both expressions describe someone extremely delighted and exultant; they are idiomatic synonyms for elation.

clue.text: Black sheep first sucked into company game

indicators.note: whatever is sucked into something ends up enclosed inside it

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
a ram is a male sheep; 'first' puts it ahead of the colour
B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black

explanation.surface: The family black sheep gets drawn into some group activity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black sheep' looks like the idiom for a disgraced relative, but the words separate; 'first' tells you the sheep comes before the colour letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Crambo is an old parlour pastime where players find rhymes for a given word, so it is a specific example of a game.

clue.text: Church leader out in Peru meeting Black Angel

indicators.note: when the leader is out, the front letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: CH is the standard abbreviation for church
the country with its first letter removed
B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black

explanation.surface: A church figure abroad in South America runs into a sinister character called the Black Angel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Church leader' wants to be a bishop or similar, but 'Church' is its own abbreviation and 'leader out' acts on Peru.
explanation.definitionFit: A cherub is one of the orders of angels in Christian tradition, so it is a specific kind of heavenly being.

clue.text: Drunk went inside almost respectable pub to start with port

indicators.note: going inside means being placed within the other letters
a drunk person staggers about, so the letters reel into a new order

parts.note: the word rearranged

indicators.note: what comes to start with is the opening letter of each word

parts.note: first letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A drunk wandered into a fairly decent bar and began with a glass of port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like the drink a tippler orders first, but it is the definition, a harbour city; 'to start with' takes the initials of three words, including 'almost'.
explanation.definitionFit: Antwerp is a major Belgian seaport on the Scheldt, so it is an example of a harbour city.

clue.text: English flower in residence leaving hotel

indicators.note: something that is leaving departs, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: a house is a residence
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An English bloom is kept in a residence after the guest leaves a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'flower' in crosswords is often something that flows, a river; the Ouse is a river in England (there are several).
explanation.definitionFit: The Ouse is a river in England, and rivers are 'flow-ers' in crossword language, so it fits an English stream.

clue.text: And another thing: change liturgical book

parts.note: a postscript (PS) adds one more thing to a letter
to alter is to change

explanation.surface: Someone adds one more demand: revise the prayer book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And another thing' sounds like a conversational interjection, but it is what a postscript does at the end of a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A psalter is a volume of the Psalms used in church services, so it is a book of worship.

clue.text: Dandy fellow — or one whose contribution is vital

parts.note: a blood is an old word for a dashing young dandy
a don is a university fellow
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fashionable man is weighed against someone whose input really matters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Or' looks like a separator between two definitions, but it is part of the wordplay; 'vital' carries its literal sense of keeping someone alive.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who gives blood supplies something life-sustaining, so their gift is literally essential to living.

clue.text: See 11
Shocks draining energy from certain forces

indicators.note: draining something empties it out, so a letter is drawn off

parts.note: sure means certain
E is the symbol for energy in physics
to prise is to force open with leverage

explanation.surface: Electric jolts sap the power of particular military units.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forces' reads as a noun for armies, but it is a verb, as in forcing a lid open.
explanation.definitionFit: Unexpected events that startle people are shocks; the two nouns are close synonyms.

clue.text: Stripped and sent, as ordered, to find water

parts.note: something stripped is bare

indicators.note: putting letters as ordered means arranging them afresh into a new sequence

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written; it doubles as part of the signal phrase

explanation.surface: Someone is stripped and dispatched under orders to go looking for water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As' does double duty, supplying two letters to be rearranged and helping signal the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The Barents Sea is part of the Arctic Ocean north of Norway and Russia, so it is a body of water.

clue.text: Men spared being in this political party

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the process of giving birth, which men never go through
second meaning: the UK party of the left

explanation.surface: A party that men are let off joining.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half reads like a jibe about a party's membership, but it means childbirth, which only women are 'in'; Labour is one of Britain's two main political parties.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the stage of giving birth and the major British centre-left party founded by trade unions.

clue.text: Reporter silent: Best sent off for holding midfielder

indicators.note: a player sent off is dispatched in disarray, so the letters are scattered and reset

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A journalist says nothing as George Best is sent off for fouling a midfielder.
explanation.walkthrough: George Best was a Manchester United winger, so 'Best sent off' reads as a red card; the punctuation hides that three words supply the letters. Nobby Stiles won the 1966 World Cup with England.
explanation.definitionFit: Stiles was a defensive midfield player for England and Manchester United, the role now called a holding midfielder, sitting in front of the back line.

clue.text: Wicked cracking safe in court interior

indicators.note: cracking something open breaks it apart, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the interior of a word is its inside letters, minus the ends

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A wicked gang is breaking into a safe inside a courthouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracking a safe' is a natural crime phrase, but 'in' belongs with the letters to be rearranged, not with the court.
explanation.definitionFit: Nefarious describes villainous, criminal or deeply immoral conduct, so it is a synonym for evil.

clue.text: Work out to get fit — that's making sense

parts.note: to reason is to work something out logically
able means fit or capable

explanation.surface: Exercising to get in shape is the sensible thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work out to get fit' reads as gym advice, but 'work out' means think through and 'fit' means capable.
explanation.definitionFit: A reasonable idea is sensible and logical, so it is one that has sound judgement behind it.

clue.text: Opera singer somewhat fat? Enormous!

indicators.note: somewhat means only partly, so just a portion of the text is used

parts.note: letters running across the two words, ignoring punctuation

explanation.surface: Is an opera singer a bit plump? No, huge!
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and exclamation break the words apart visually, but the letters run straight across them.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenor is the highest standard adult male voice, a common lead role in operatic works.

clue.text: Wind, destructive at the outset, coming in closer

indicators.note: coming in means entering, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: closer in the sense of stingier, tight-fisted

indicators.note: what comes at the outset is the opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A gale that is destructive from the start is drawing nearer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind' looks like a gale, but it is the verb rhyming with 'find'; 'closer' means more tight-fisted, not nearer.
explanation.definitionFit: A path or river that winds follows a twisting, looping course, which is exactly what to meander describes.

clue.text: Somehow blame Nellie's peach dessert?

indicators.note: somehow suggests an unspecified way of rearranging, so the letters are shuffled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Whoever is at fault, Nellie gets blamed for the peach pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: Peach Melba was named after the soprano Dame Nellie Melba; the question mark admits the answer is her name rather than the whole dish.
explanation.definitionFit: The singer's surname identifies the classic dessert of peaches, raspberry sauce and ice cream created in her honour.

clue.text: See 11
Fibre fine served with Scandinavian fish

parts.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
lax is the Swedish and Norwegian word for salmon

explanation.surface: Good roughage comes with a plate of Nordic fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a menu with dietary fibre, but 'Fibre' is the plant textile and 'fine' is a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Flax is the plant whose stem threads are spun into linen, so it is a textile strand source.

clue.text: Duty (and where it often lies)

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a responsibility or burden
second meaning: read as two words, the place a duty falls

explanation.surface: A reflection on obligation and who ends up carrying it.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as ON US: a duty often lies on us, which is why the phrase is in brackets as an aside.
explanation.definitionFit: An onus is a burden of responsibility, the obligation that someone is expected to carry out.

clue.text: The elegantly stylish 11 15 7?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: old British slang for smart or chic
second meaning: the nickname of the footballer whose full name fills 11, 15 and 7 across

explanation.walkthrough: Norbert Peter Stiles, England's 1966 World Cup midfielder, was always known as Nobby; the question mark admits that the toothless hard man was hardly elegant.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means fashionably smart in dated British slang, and it is also the familiar nickname given to anyone called Norbert.

clue.text: Arch rival in Tyneside canteen, one gathered?

parts.note: Tyneside is in the North East, NE

indicators.note: something gathered is taken in and held, so it sits inside another piece

parts.note: a mess is a military canteen
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Your greatest enemy turns up in a Newcastle works canteen as one of the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it places the rival in the canteen, but it only links; Tyneside is the Newcastle area of North East England.
explanation.definitionFit: A nemesis is a long-standing opponent who seems destined to defeat you, the main adversary.

clue.text: Unusually frosty north: underwear needed

indicators.note: something done unusually departs from the normal order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
N is the compass abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: It is exceptionally cold up north, so you will need warm underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: Y-fronts are British men's briefs with an upside-down Y-shaped front opening.
explanation.definitionFit: Y-fronts are a style of men's briefs, so they are an example of undergarments.

clue.text: Roll stuffed with old chicken

indicators.note: something stuffed with filling has that filling inside it

parts.note: a roster is a roll or list of names
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A bread roll filled with leftover chicken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roll' looks like bread to go with the chicken filling, but it is a list of names.
explanation.definitionFit: A rooster is a male domestic fowl, so it is one kind of chicken.

clue.text: Provides force with crossing when laying siege

indicators.note: an army laying siege surrounds a place on all sides

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
F is the symbol for force in physics
a ford is a shallow river crossing

explanation.surface: An army sends troops across a river while besieging a town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Force' and 'crossing' read as military terms, but they are a physics symbol and a shallow place in a river.
explanation.definitionFit: To afford can mean to supply or offer, as in 'the window affords a view', so it matches gives.

clue.text: Secretive person in the pink

definitions.meaning: first meaning: someone who keeps tightly closed, like a shellfish

definitions.note: names a shade, as in oyster pink
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a pale pinkish-grey colour

explanation.walkthrough: 'In the pink' looks like the idiom for being healthy, but it is split so 'the pink' points at a colour shade.
explanation.definitionFit: A closed shellfish is the image for someone who reveals nothing, and the shellfish's name also describes a pale pinkish-grey tint.

clue.text: Cursed mother to Scots hooligan

parts.note: a dam is an animal's mother
a ned is a young Scottish lout

explanation.surface: A mother swears at a Glasgow thug.
explanation.walkthrough: Ned is Scottish slang for a young hooligan.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone damned has been condemned or put under a curse, so the two adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Boat captain initially lost authority

indicators.note: something lost is gone, so that letter disappears

parts.note: a coracle is a small round wicker boat

indicators.note: initially points to what comes first, the opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: The skipper of a vessel at first loses his command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' picks the first letter of 'captain', and that letter comes off the front of the little boat.
explanation.definitionFit: An oracle is a person regarded as an infallible source of wisdom, someone whose word is trusted, an expert.

clue.text: German fellow shows bum after stripping

indicators.note: stripping peels off the outside, leaving the inner letters

parts.note: bum is bottom; with its outer letters removed

explanation.surface: A German man bares his backside once he has undressed.
explanation.walkthrough: The source word is a synonym, BOTTOM, not 'bum' itself; stripping it of its ends leaves a common German first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto is a traditional German masculine first name, so it identifies a man from Germany.

clue.text: Schedule this month one absolutely fixed

parts.note: to set a date is to schedule it
inst. (instant) is the old business abbreviation for this month
taken as written

explanation.surface: Book one appointment this month that cannot be moved.
explanation.walkthrough: INST, short for 'instant', is the dated commercial-letter abbreviation meaning of the current month.
explanation.definitionFit: Something carved permanently cannot be altered, so the idiom describes plans that are unchangeable.

clue.text: Flavoured sausage regrettably returned with note

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so it runs backwards

parts.note: alas expresses regret
mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A spicy sausage sadly sent back with a complaint note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' looks like a written message attached to a return, but it is a musical sol-fa syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: Salami is a cured Italian meat seasoned with garlic and spices, a well-known highly seasoned sausage.

clue.text: Patronised and offended in South Atlantic

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south

indicators.note: being in something means sitting within it

parts.note: 'the pond' is a jokey name for the Atlantic
sore means aggrieved or offended

explanation.surface: Someone is talked down to and upset while out in the South Atlantic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patronised' suggests condescension, but it means supported financially; 'South Atlantic' splits into a compass letter and 'the pond'.
explanation.definitionFit: To patronise originally means to support as a patron, which is what a backer does when funding an event.
